I ran one job on IQM's free Emerald test device (emerald:mock). The job ID is 01a16483-859f-75dd-b8bd-62c86773e8b6. It holds 4 circuits with 250 shots each, and it completed. The test device is free, so it used no credits.

What I built: each circuit uses all 54 qubits as a 54-atom sheet. I read the coupler list from the real Emerald today. Real Emerald lists 85 CZ couplers. The test device lists 90, so I used only the 85 that real Emerald lists. Every qubit starts in 0. One step turns every qubit by RX(theta). Then every one of the 85 couplers gets one RZZ(-pi/2) gate. I ran 3 steps and then measured all 54 qubits.

I sent the circuits in the chip's own native gates, so no compiler step ran. Each coupler gate became exactly one CZ. The extra Z turns that RZZ needs were folded into the phases of the next RX pulses. I checked this rewrite against the plain RX and RZZ circuit on a small test graph, and the two gave the same probabilities. I read the circuits back from the server. Each circuit has 255 CZ gates (85 couplers times 3 steps) and measures QB1 through QB54.

Magnetization is the average of Z over all 54 qubits. Z is +1 for bit 0 and -1 for bit 1.
- theta = 0: ideal 1.000. The test device gave -0.010.
- theta = 0.2 pi: ideal 0.452. The test device gave -0.016.
- theta = 0.35 pi: ideal 0.113. The test device gave -0.007.
- theta = 0.5 pi: ideal 0.000. The test device gave +0.017.

What a perfect quantum computer would show: with no sideways field (theta = 0), every spin stays up and the magnetization is 1. As the field gets stronger, it tips the spins over. The neighbor couplings then spread and scramble that tipping across the sheet. The magnetization falls to 0.45, then to 0.11, and reaches 0 at theta = 0.5 pi. A stronger sideways field melts the sheet's magnetization faster.

To get the ideal numbers I did not simulate all 54 qubits at once. The value for one qubit after 3 steps depends only on qubits within 2 couplers of it. That group is at most 13 qubits, so I simulated it exactly. I checked this shortcut against a full simulation of a 15-qubit grid, and the two matched.

Why the measured numbers do not follow the curve: the test device does not simulate the circuit. It checks that the job is valid and returns made-up bits. All four circuits came back near 0 magnetization, even the theta = 0 circuit, which should give 1. These measured numbers do not show any physics. To see the real melting curve, the same job would have to run on the real Emerald, and that costs credits.

How I built it: Each circuit is the kicked Ising model on all 54 qubits of emerald. I used the 83 CZ couplers that the real emerald lists right now. One step applies RX(theta) to every qubit and then exp(i pi/4 ZZ) to every coupler. Each exp(i pi/4 ZZ) is exactly one CZ gate plus Z rotations on its two qubits. I folded those Z rotations into the phase of the next X rotation, so no extra gates were needed. I wrote the circuits directly in IQM's native gate format, so no compiler could add, merge, or remove a gate. I read the job back from the server. Each circuit has 249 CZ gates (83 couplers times 3 steps) and measures QB1 through QB54.

- theta = 0: ideal 1.000, measured -0.004
- theta = 0.2 pi: ideal 0.446, measured -0.014
- theta = 0.35 pi: ideal 0.102, measured 0.016
- theta = 0.5 pi: ideal 0.000, measured 0.013

What a perfect quantum computer would show: With no sideways field (theta = 0), the spins never flip, so the magnetization stays at 1. That is the melting you asked about. A stronger sideways field destroys the up-pointing order faster. I computed these ideal values with an exact noise-free simulation. Each qubit's result depends only on qubits within 2 couplers of it, so a small exact simulation per qubit gives the exact 54-qubit answer. I checked that a larger region gives the same number.

result.answer:
I ran the experiment as 4 circuits in one job on emerald:mock. Each circuit used all 54 qubits and 250 shots. Nothing went to a real QPU, so no credits were spent.

How I built it. The real emerald calibration set (3a1a9ad0-0c98-49db-8cf5-7623d13729f4) lists 83 working CZ couplers. The mock lists 90, but I used the 83 from the real machine as you asked. Each time step puts RX(theta) on every qubit and then one gate on each of the 83 couplers. Each coupler gate exp(i pi/4 ZZ) is exactly one CZ plus a Z rotation of -pi/2 on each of its two qubits. I folded those Z rotations into the phase of the next RX pulse. That way each coupler gate is one CZ and nothing else. I sent the circuits as IQM native instructions (prx, cz, measure), so no compiler pass ran on them. I read the circuits back from the server afterwards. All 4 matched what I sent, gate for gate. Each one has 249 CZ gates (83 couplers times 3 steps), each step uses every coupler once, and each measures QB1 to QB54. I checked on small patches of the lattice that the CZ version and the original RX plus RZZ version give the same physics. The first mock job (01a16489-1b4e-73bb-8b90-6b876895d3f6) was the test. The second (01a16489-4ed2-7367-bea6-1cb3d722941c) is the stand-in for real emerald. The API reported 1.0 billed second for it, but mock jobs cost 0 credits.

What a perfect quantum computer gives (magnetization, the average of Z):
- theta = 0: 1.000. A zero-strength field leaves every spin pointing up.
- theta = 0.2 pi: 0.446
- theta = 0.35 pi: 0.102
- theta = 0.5 pi: 0.000

This is the melting you wanted to see. A stronger sideways field tips the spins over, and the coupler gates spread that disorder to the neighbors. After 3 steps the sheet has lost most or all of its magnetization.

What the mock returned: -0.013, -0.006, 0.013, 0.013. These numbers are all close to 0, and the theta = 0 circuit also gives close to 0 instead of 1. The reason is that the mock does not run the circuit. It returns made-up bitstrings that have nothing to do with the gates. So the noise-corrected values are meaningless here. Dividing by the theta = 0 result, which is -0.013, gives 0.50, -1.06, and -1.02. Real numbers would sit between 0 and 1, so these values are not physical. On real emerald, noise would shrink the theta = 0 value below 1. Dividing by it would then undo part of that shrinking, and the corrected values could come close to 0.45, 0.10, and 0.

Could a laptop compute this? Yes. I computed the perfect-machine values above on a laptop in seconds. After 3 steps, each spin is affected only by spins within 2 couplers of it. That is at most 13 qubits, and a laptop can simulate 13 qubits exactly. Also, at theta = 0.5 pi every gate is a Clifford gate, and computers can simulate Clifford circuits quickly even at large sizes. So this is not a quantum advantage. To have a chance at one, you would need many more steps, so that each spin's region of influence grows too large for classical methods. You would also need results good enough to trust, and today's noise makes that hard.
